title: Designing Experiments to Tell What Neurons Actually Encode
one_liner: Use information theory to find the exact tasks that reveal whether neurons encode raw sensory patterns or knowledge-adjusted patterns.
lead: Brains solve problems under uncertainty, combining what they see with what they already know. Two competing theories disagree on how neurons store this knowledge: one says they store raw sensory patterns only, the other says they store the combination. This paper shows how to design experiments that definitively prove which theory is right.

paras: Imagine you hear a faint noise in the dark. Your brain combines two things: what you actually hear right now (the raw data) plus what you already know about the world (a faint noise is more likely a car horn than a chainsaw). Two competing theories explain how neurons store this knowledge. The raw-pattern theory says neurons write down only the sensory data, like a camera recording what you hear. The knowledge-adjusted theory says neurons write down the final guess that combines data with what you know, like a weatherman combining raw measurements with historical patterns.

A naive experiment would play sounds and ask subjects to guess what made them. But both theories would pass this test equally well, because both make humans answer correctly. The real problem is that no one knows how to design an experiment where the two theories predict different answers. The paper solves this: it finds the exact task design that makes each theory wrong in a distinctive way.

callout.html: Find the specific tasks where raw-pattern-coding and knowledge-adjusted-pattern-coding neurons give contradictory answers.

panels.title: 1. Two competing theories
panels.viz_args: Theory A: raw data only; Theory B: data plus knowledge
panels.caption: Neurons either store raw sensory patterns or sensory plus prior knowledge.

panels.title: 2. Naive experiment fails
panels.caption: Both theories give the same answer to normal tasks, so you learn nothing.

panels.title: 3. Information gap
panels.caption: Theory A's decoder shines on raw-biased tasks; Theory B's shines on knowledge-biased tasks.

panels.title: 4. Optimizing task design
panels.viz_args: Prior context A vs B; stimulus skewed to maximize gap
panels.caption: Change the prior knowledge and stimulus mix to widen the prediction disagreement.

panels.title: 5. Experiment reveals the truth
panels.caption: The decoder that wins tells you which theory the neurons are using.

steps.text: Likelihood encoding (raw sensory patterns only) versus posterior encoding (sensory plus prior knowledge).
Design neural network decoders that look for one kind of information and measure error when each decoder tries to read the wrong thing.
Compute the expected difference in decoder error when likelihood decoder reads likelihood-coded neurons versus when it reads posterior-coded neurons, using KL divergence math.
Vary the task parameters (prior odds, stimulus distribution, contrast level) to find the task design that widens the gap most.
Collect actual neural data under that task design; which decoder wins shows which coding hypothesis the real neurons use.

paras: The paper changes the task stimulus distribution—the mix and probability of sensory patterns subjects see during an experiment. Instead of using a generic, neutral task that both theories pass equally, it finds the exact distribution that creates a gap where each theory predicts different neural responses. A standard experiment might show orientation gratings equally often; this paper reweights them so that some orientations become rare in one context and common in another, forcing the learned world-knowledge (prior, what the brain already knew before the task started) to push harder against the sensory data.

hidden.h2: The information gap—measuring mismatch between theories
hidden.name: expected decoder performance difference
paras: The information gap is the expected performance gap when you try to read the wrong kind of information from neurons. If a population actually encodes likelihood functions (raw sensory patterns), a decoder designed to read likelihood will do well, but a decoder looking for posterior information will fail with high error. The gap is the difference in their errors. Measuring it tells you which hypothesis the neurons are actually using.

The paper estimates this gap by computing how much a task-marginalized surrogate posterior (what the true posterior looks like when you average over all possible tasks) differs from the true posterior. That difference, measured as KL divergence (a distance metric between two probability distributions), predicts decoder performance differences across all task settings.

heat.caption: Darker means stronger mismatch between what the decoder expects and what neurons actually encode. Highlighted cells show the scenarios where the paper gets maximum signal.

reads.html: The information gap is how much better one decoder does than the other on neurons of unknown type, because the two theories predict different neural firing patterns—one decoder will match those patterns perfectly while the other will fail, creating a gap in error rates. High gap means the two theories predict very different neural patterns; low gap means they agree, so the experiment teaches nothing.

Information gap is the expected error difference between an optimal likelihood decoder and an optimal posterior decoder applied to populations hypothesized to encode either likelihood functions or posterior distributions, derived by evaluating KL divergence between true and task-marginalized surrogate posteriors.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: the mismatch forces the truth out
paras: The mechanism is simple: if neurons truly encode likelihood (raw patterns), then asking them a posterior question fails. The decoder looking for posterior information gets the wrong thing and suffers high error. The reverse happens with posterior-coding neurons. By designing the task so the two theories disagree maximally, you guarantee that actual neural data will show which decoder wins, proving which coding scheme the brain uses.

The paper optimizes by varying two knobs. First, it changes the prior knowledge (context): maybe in one half of the experiment, the world tends to have high-contrast stimuli, and in the other half, low-contrast. Neurons that truly encode the posterior will fire differently in each context (because prior changes), but likelihood-coding neurons stay the same. Second, it shifts the stimulus distribution within each context. Some orientations become rarer in context A, commoner in context B. This forces the prior to push against the sensory data more aggressively. Together, these moves widen the gap between what likelihood and posterior decoders predict, making the experiment maximally informative.

stages.s: Neural responses to two contexts with different prior knowledge
Train likelihood decoder: extract raw stimulus patterns from the neural data
Train posterior decoder: extract stimulus patterns adjusted by context prior
Measure error for each decoder on held-out neural data
Compute information gap: difference in decoder errors
Optimal task parameters that maximize gap for maximum discriminative power

math.words: Information gap is the expected cross-entropy loss difference between the optimal posterior decoder and the optimal likelihood decoder, derived from the KL divergence between the true posterior and a task-averaged surrogate posterior.
math.equation: Delta_info_L = E[CE_loss(g_P, r_L)] - E[CE_loss(g_L, r_L)] = E[KL(p_true | p_marginal)]
symbols: the information gap for likelihood-coding hypothesis
cross-entropy loss when posterior decoder g_P reads likelihood-coded neurons r_L
cross-entropy loss when likelihood decoder g_L reads likelihood-coded neurons r_L
KL divergence between true posterior and task-marginalized surrogate posterior
expected value averaged over all trials

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Imagine a likelihood-coding neuron population with true likelihood encoding.
A likelihood decoder tries to extract orientation: 100 trials, error = 0.2 (good match).
A posterior decoder tries to extract orientation adjusted by prior: 100 trials, error = 1.8 (bad mismatch).
Information gap = 1.8 - 0.2 = 1.6 (strong signal that neurons encode likelihood).
Now test a posterior-coding population: likelihood decoder error = 1.9, posterior decoder error = 0.3.
Information gap = 0.3 - 1.9 = -1.6 (strong signal in opposite direction, proving posterior coding).
The task that achieves this ±1.6 gap is the one the paper finds by maximizing KL divergence.

math.note: The KL divergence between true and marginal posteriors tells you how hard the prior pulls against the sensory data; larger divergence means larger gap, so maximizing divergence finds the task design with maximum experiment discriminative power.

bars.h2: Decoder performance on each neuron type

charts.title: Likelihood-coding neurons
charts.note: Likelihood decoder shines; posterior decoder fails because it looks for prior modulation that does not exist in the neural data.

charts.title: Posterior-coding neurons
charts.note: Posterior decoder shines; likelihood decoder fails because prior information is mixed into every response.

charts.title: With optimized task design
charts.note: Optimizing stimulus prior and distribution makes the gap bigger and more reliable, because larger gaps mean the error difference between decoders is unmistakable, so each trial carries more information about which hypothesis is true, and fewer trials reach statistical certainty.

items.html: If the neural network decoders are poorly trained or under-parameterized, they fail to extract either kind of information well, washing out the gap. You must fit the decoders carefully and validate that they achieve near-optimal performance on synthetic ground-truth data before running the actual experiment.

items.b: Task design is not realized in the lab
items.html: The optimal task distribution is calculated mathematically, but in a real experiment the context priors or stimulus distributions might drift or not match the theory. If the prior is weaker than designed, the gap shrinks and the experiment loses power.

items.b: Neurons encode a mixture of both
items.html: Real neural populations might partly encode likelihood and partly encode posterior. The information gap still works, but the gap becomes smaller and the experiment needs more trials to reach a conclusion.

The paper shows that optimal task design depends on stimulus contrast level. If the lab uses a different contrast than the theory predicts, the gap may not reach its theoretical maximum and the experiment power degrades.

Carefully calibrate decoders on synthetic data; measure and match the actual prior odds and stimulus distribution in the behavioral task to the mathematical design; scale contrast to match the theory; collect enough trials to resolve the gap signal reliably.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: The demo should simulate a two-context orientation discrimination task with either likelihood-coding neurons or posterior-coding neurons (ground truth). Then fit two decoders: one trained to extract orientation from the neural responses, and one trained to extract orientation adjusted by the context prior. The demo sweeps the context frequencies and stimulus distributions, computing the information gap at each step, and finds the parameters that maximize it. Finally, it measures decoder performance on held-out neural data and shows that the decoder matching the true encoding wins by the predicted amount.
demo.metric_eq: information gap = cross-entropy loss of mismatched decoder - cross-entropy loss of matched decoder
demo.closing: The core claim is this: when you run the optimized task, the decoder matching the true neural encoding outperforms the other by the predicted gap, because the task design amplifies the coding difference so that one decoder's assumptions match the neural firing patterns while the other's do not. If you reverse the ground truth from likelihood to posterior coding, the winner flips and the gap sign reverses, proving the method discriminates.
